articles.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6.1 Sol with near-Astra performance at one-fifth the cost
articles.summary: OpenAI has introduced GPT-6.1 Sol, an upgraded version of GPT-6 Sol designed to deliver stronger performance across coding, professional work, computer
articles.body: OpenAI has introduced GPT-6.1 Sol, an upgraded version of GPT-6 Sol designed to deliver stronger performance across coding, professional work, computer use and scientific research at a lower cost. The company says GPT-6.1 Sol can approach the intelligence of its more capable GPT-6 Astra model on several tasks while costing about one-fifth as much. The new model is priced at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. Cached input costs just $0.10 per million tokens, which OpenAI says is 95% lower than standard input pricing and 50% lower than GPT-6 Sol's cached input price.For comparison, GPT-6 Astra costs $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens, while GPT-6 Luna is priced at $0.10 and $0.50 respectively.GPT-6.1 Sol offers stronger coding and professional workOpenAI says GPT-6.1 Sol matches GPT-6 Astra on the DeepSWE v1.1 software-engineering test at roughly one-fifth of the cost. It also improves on GPT-6 Sol's best score by 6.4 percentage points while using a lower reasoning effort. On GDP.pdf, which tests how well AI models answer questions based on complex professional documents, GPT-6.1 Sol scored higher than Opus 5.5 with fallbacks at less than half the cost per task. It also came close to GPT-6 Astra's performance at around one-fifth the cost.On AutomationBench, which tests multi-step business workflows, GPT-6.1 Sol scored 2.2 percentage points higher than Opus 5.5 at medium reasoning effort while costing about one-third as much.The model also improved on OSWorld 2.0, a benchmark for computer-use tasks. OpenAI says GPT-6.1 Sol scored seven percentage points higher than GPT-6 Sol at maximum reasoning effort and came within 2.1 points of GPT-6 Astra.For scientific research, GPT-6.1 Sol more than doubled GPT-6 Sol's score on Terminal-Bench Science 0.1 at maximum reasoning effort. Its average cost per task was $5.47, compared with $23.80 for GPT-6 Astra. OpenAI also reported a reduction in factual errors on difficult prompts, from 11.4% with GPT-6 Sol to 7.7% with GPT-6.1 Sol.GPT‑6.1 Sol pricing and availabilityGPT‑6.1 Sol is available starting today to all Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex. GPT‑6.1 Sol is not yet available in Chat. Developers can also access it through the OpenAI API as gpt-6.1-sol. Its standard API prices are $2 per million input tokens, $0.10 per million cached input tokens, and $10 per million output tokens.OpenAI said that it will offer GPT‑6.1 Sol Ultrafast⁠, with up to 8x faster token generation compared to its standard speed in Codex in the coming days.You use AI every day. articles.title: Regulating AI 'not the right place to start' says Bank of England governor
articles.summary: AI needs "rigorous" testing and safeguards to contain risk, Andrew Bailey says.
articles.body:
The Governor of the Bank of England has said regulating artificial intelligence (AI) "is not the right place to start" but instead called first for "rigorous" testing to find vulnerabilities and safeguards to contain risk.

Writing his first-ever article for Substack, Andrew Bailey said the risks around AI were "real and increasingly significant".

Bailey said the development of AI should not be halted or prohibited - "on the contrary, the benefits are immense" - but added there must be a system for intervention and to establish boundaries in which AI operates.

In recent weeks, the debate about the potential risks surrounding the rapid development of AI and what it means for humanity has intensified.

The bosses of leading AI firms such as Anthropic and OpenAI have called for development of the technology to slow down and for an internationally co-ordinated approach assessing risks and putting safeguards in place.

OpenAI recently announced that it would not release its latest AI model due to safety concerns .

The idea of a slowdown, however, has been rejected by the likes of President Donald Trump who has said the US is leading the AI race ahead of China, adding: "And, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins."

But on Tuesday, after hosting a summit with the leading firms in AI such as OpenAI and Anthropic, Trump said executives had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks.

Chinese AI tool told researchers how to make bioweapons

OpenAI scraps rollout of new model over safety concerns

Under the agreement, the companies are responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.

In the UK, Bailey said "important work" was underway in testing AI - the UK has set up the AI Security Institute - which, he said, should help form part of a set of standards.

"But the pace of progress must accelerate," the bank governor said, though he added: "We should proceed with a degree of humility."

He said, with testing, there will be failures and "models will behave unexpectedly".

But, he said: "That is not evidence that testing has failed, rather it is evidence of why testing is necessary."

Bailey said that testing should not be seen as an alternative to future regulation - over time a more formal regulatory framework might emerge. "But regulation is not, in my view, the right place to start."

articles.title: HPE Gets $1.2 Billion AMD Gear Order From Vultr in Latest AI Win
articles.summary: Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. won a $1.2 billion order to provide Advanced Micro Devices Inc. server racks with HPE networking gear to cloud company Vultr.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. won a $1.2 billion order to provide Advanced Micro Devices Inc. server racks with HPE networking gear to cloud company Vultr.

HPE will deploy AMD's Helios AI racks, which contain chips for artificial intelligence work and use HPE's networking switches and software, in US data centers belonging to Vultr, a West Palm Beach, Florida-based cloud provider. This represents HPE's first order for these systems.

Vultr worked for three years with Juniper Networks, which was acquired by HPE in 2025. The cloud provider is backed by AMD.

HPE, one of the largest makers of computing equipment, has become a key beneficiary of demand for hardware to develop and deploy artificial intelligence. Its shares have more than doubled this year, fueled by its AI prospects.

articles.title: Airbnb adds AI search, more social features
articles.summary: Airbnb is also launching new services such as meal delivery and laundry in select locations.
articles.body:
Airbnb is evolving in two directions: On the ground, it wants to compete with hotels by providing myriad services; online, it is using AI and people in its Airbnb network to aid travel discovery.

As part of its fall product update, the company is adding services to the app it had launched last year, such as meal delivery, laundry, baby-gear rental, ski and boat rental in limited locations, and expanded grocery delivery.

The second big feature is AI search. The company has taken a cautious approach to rolling out AI features, with CEO Brian Chesky opting to stay away from a chatbot-like interface . Earlier this year, he teased the new search feature for property discovery .

Now, users can switch on a toggle to search for properties via text or voice prompts. Once you start the search, the interface will show you dynamic filters based on your preferences. For instance, if you type “baby” in the AI search filter, Airbnb will automatically show you further filters like cribs, playgrounds, or children’s books and toys.

The platform is also using AI to bring out relevant features of a property, and will let you compare properties in your wish list by way of AI-powered summaries and reviews.

“We are finally making our first foray into AI search. And what you see is just the very beginning of something. And over the coming months, we’re going to really be iterating this very quickly. It’s not hard to create AI search; it’s hard to create AI search in e-commerce when you have $100 billion going through your platform,” Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky told TechCrunch.

“Anyone can vibe-code a search function, but to do something that doesn’t kill conversion rate, that’s the hard part.”

The company is also doubling down on social features that nudge people to take more trips and book additional experiences such as food tastings and craft workshops. Last year, the app started allowing users to connect with fellow travelers and friends on its platform.

Now, travelers can look at a map based on their connections’ past or upcoming trips. When you tap on a trip, you can see where your connection stayed, and which experiences they sought out. For those conscious about their privacy, there’s an option to not share their trips with others as well.

Airbnb is also building pages about neighborhoods based on guest reviews and other sources to help travelers discover places to eat and things to do.

articles.title: Two Google alumni raise $11.3M to back AI startups that enterprises will actually pay for
articles.summary: BAG Ventures announces close of a $11.3M Fund I to invest in all things AI.
articles.body:
Two Google alumni have closed an $11.3 million fund to back early-stage AI startups, betting that the era of enterprise AI experimentation is ending and that customers will increasingly pay only for products that prove their worth.

BAG Ventures , founded by Bonita Stewart, a former Google vice president, and Jackson Georges Jr., a former CapitalG partner, closed the fund after about two years of investing from it as it came together. The firm has already backed 10 companies, including the software company SXD, the AI travel agent BizTrip, and the agentic reasoning platform Nomadic.

It invests in startups in areas like AI infrastructure, compute, physical and edge AI, security, governance, and vertical SaaS. Check sizes range from $100,000 to $500,000, and the team hopes to invest the rest of the fund over the next two years.

Stewart spent 17 years at Google, including nearly a decade as a vice president. During that time, she also served on the board of Gradient Ventures, Google's early-stage AI fund. She is a limited partner in the Female Founders Fund and the Operator Collective. With Georges, she also co-led the angel syndicate BAG Collective, which has more than 450 members.

Georges worked at GE Healthcare and at Google, where he met Stewart. He later became a partner at CapitalG, Alphabet's growth fund. He and Stewart were in the first cohort of the Black Venture Institute at Berkeley.

The pair say their edge is access. They launched BAG Ventures to "address the emerging AI divide between founders and operators," Georges said.

"Founders needed inside access to the organizations they wanted to sell into, and we knew so many high-level operators who wanted to support early founders but didn't know how," he said. As a result, "we don't just give founders capital; we give them direct warm introductions to potential customers and hands-on [go-to-market] advice," he continued, adding that the firm, whose limited partners include Google, as well as operators from Nvidia, Amazon, and Snowflake, has more than 150 limited partners altogether at a wide range of companies.

"Lots of firms have an operator network," Georges said. "We want to be one that's genuinely useful."

Georges' investing thesis rests on a shift he sees in how enterprises buy AI. He said the "experimental sandbox" phase is ending. "Enterprises are dialing in heavily on the unit economics right now," he noted. "They aren't just paying for open-ended chatbots anymore; they are paying for deterministic solutions. The real value is coming from solutions that integrate deeply into legacy workflows and actually execute the work." Examples include automating code reviews and parsing legal documents.

articles.title: Here’s how tech leaders will self-police AI safety under Trump’s deal
articles.summary: The full AI safety deal in which top executives agreed to self-regulate their artificial intelligence technology contains four vague, common-sense guidelines.
articles.body: We now have the full details of the “morally binding” AI safety deal announced by President Trump yesterday, in which top executives agreed to self-regulate their artificial intelligence technology. The accord, officially titled the Joint Commitment On Frontier Responsibilities, was shared online by tech founder and presidential advisor David Sacks, and has been signed by Google’s Sundar Pichai, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, XAI’s Elon Musk, and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. “In order to build a positive future for the American people and the world, we believe every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely and in a way that builds trust with customers and the public,” reads the opening line of the document. “The participating companies will meet regularly to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems.” The agreement outlines four rules for each company that aim to ensure frontier AI models behave as intended, and that any problems are quickly identified and resolved: > 1) Implement robust internal controls to monitor the capabilities and alignment of its models during training and deployment around areas like cybersecurity, biosecurity, and chemical threats, and to ensure that its models do not hack or access technical systems in unintended ways. > 2) Empower an internal team to ensure all of the controls, monitoring, and detection are operating as intended, and that any issues are remediated. > 3) Partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator to carry out independent assessments of whether the controls, monitoring, and detection are operating as intended. > 4) Designate an independent committee of the board of directors to oversee and receive reports from the teams operating the controls and the internal and external auditors and evaluators, as well as to ensure any issues identified are remediated. The agreement says these steps will give the companies, their users, and the general public — which have mounting concerns around AI safety — “confidence that the technology is operating as intended.” A later passage also says that “over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations.” In their current state, these rules are mostly vague, common-sense safety procedures for any tech company, and don’t mention any penalties for violating the agreement, making this little more than a pinky promise from AI leaders to do the bare minimum. And that’s despite Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic having all violated that first rule over the last few months when their AIs went rogue and hacked other companies and even government websites. Trump introduced the deal yesterday at the same time as ordering the US government to refer to AI as ‘Super Intelligence’ going forward, reasoning that the word “artificial” sounds bad and “super is the best word of all.” Alongside the tech oligarchs, Trump added his own signature to the AI safety agreement, with his title listed as “President of the Unites States.”

articles.title: 100 million deaths can't be settled with a lawsuit, Bill Gates rejects argument that AI companies can police themselves; says: I almost can't keep a...
articles.summary: Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has rejected the idea that lawsuits and market pressure can keep artificial intelligence companies in check.
articles.body: Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has rejected the idea that lawsuits and market pressure can keep artificial intelligence companies in check. Asked why product liability and reputational damage aren't enough to stop firms from releasing dangerous AI, Gates answered with a question of his own. "So say you kill 100 million people, you want to use a lawsuit?" he said on "The Ezra Klein Show." "I almost can't keep a straight face."The episode was released on September 29, the same day US President Donald Trump and the heads of the largest AI companies signed a voluntary safety pact at the White House. The pact carries no legal penalties. Gates, who titled a 2023 essay "The Risks of AI Are Real but Manageable," now calls AI the most dangerous thing humans have ever gone near.Bill Gates says AI can already help bioterrorists and hackersHost Ezra Klein put to Gates a view voiced by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang: if a product is unsafe, the CEO simply shouldn't launch it, and no new laws are needed. Klein added that Trump and David Sacks, who has advised the President on AI, hold a similar position.Gates disagreed. He said AI can already help a bioterrorist kill hundreds of millions of people, or carry out a cyberattack that scrambles bank accounts and shuts down a power grid. "We crossed the cyber threshold and we crossed the bio threshold early this year," he said.He pointed to the models leading up to Anthropic's Mythos, which he said were finding security bugs in code that humans had checked for over 20 years.Why lawsuits won't keep people safe from AI, according to GatesGates compared the self-policing argument to scrapping the rules for other risky industries. Drugs need regulatory approval, airlines answer to a safety board and cars must have seatbelts, he said. Nobody proposes waiting to sue opioid makers after the damage is done.He also brushed aside the claim that built-in filters fix the problem. Anyone can take an open-source model capable of designing bioweapons and switch off its monitoring, he said."You can't rely on the industry to self-regulate here," Gates added. "I mean, it's just insane."What Bill Gates wants instead of AI self-regulationGates is calling for a mandatory supervisory layer of safeguards and monitoring across all AI models, and argued it would not meaningfully slow development. Open-source models could stay free and customisable, but would need to run on platforms where governments can confirm the monitoring hasn't been stripped out.He has little patience for the argument that regulation would hand China the lead. "I don't know what it means to 'win,'" he said, adding that neither the US nor China can win over the other.He also said the balance can tip too far the other way. Anthropic's Mythos and Fable models, according to Gates, are tuned so strictly that users asking about cancer end up falling back on the company's smaller models.Gates' warning lands as Trump and AI CEOs sign a voluntary safety pactThe White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities was signed by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Huang and xAI founder Elon Musk. It sets out four layers of checks: internal controls, an internal safety team, independent external auditors and board-level oversight. Trump called it "almost like a constitution," though the agreement appears to let companies pick their own auditors and cannot be enforced by law.Gates had raised the stakes two days earlier, telling a US television interviewer that AI in the wrong hands is powerful enough to drive events that cause "a billion deaths."The choice he put to Klein was whether the world waits for a major cyber or bio attack before making safeguards mandatory, or puts them in place before millions die.You use AI every day. articles.title: O’Reilly: ‘I think you’re going to have to have a new police agency’ for AI
articles.summary: Political commentator Bill O’Reilly on Tuesday called for a new federal law enforcement agency dedicated to artificial intelligence, arguing that the AI industry’s ability to police itself would not go far enough to address the technology’s potential dangers. “I think you’re going to have a new police agency, federal, that all they do is look…
articles.body:
Political commentator Bill O’Reilly on Tuesday called for a new federal law enforcement agency dedicated to artificial intelligence, arguing that the AI industry’s ability to police itself would not go far enough to address the technology’s potential dangers .

“I think you’re going to have a new police agency, federal, that all they do is look at AI,” O’Reilly said in an appearance on NewsNation’s “Katie Pavlich Tonight.”

A series of rogue AI incidents , including OpenAI’s recent breach of federal government websites, led to calls from industry experts and leaders about the need to establish safeguards around the rapidly growing technology.

President Trump recently announced plans to establish an “AI Force” and appoint an “AI czar.” The president has, however, rejected calls for regulation , which he argued could slow U.S. development of the tech in the global race for AI dominance.

O’Reilly agreed with Trump that the U.S. faces pressure to continue to rapidly develop AI — which the president is seeking to rebrand as “superintelligence” after signing an executive order Tuesday — as it competes with China.

“We have to be first in this arms race,” he said. “You can’t let China do whatever they want to do.”

Trump also said the government could identify misuse of AI “very easily” through the country’s existing criminal and civil justice system.

The former Fox News host argued Tuesday that a dedicated federal agency would be necessary as increasingly powerful AI systems create new opportunities for cybercrime and other threats.

“The ability to commit crimes, extortion, theft, even trying to get nuclear codes, messing around with the weaponry, it’s all going to get worse,” he continued. “And so, to me, I want to be as preventative as possible.”

O’Reilly added that the federal government should take a more active role in preventing criminal groups from eventually gaining access to incredibly powerful AI systems.

His comments come the same day Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) announced that some of the country’s largest AI companies had signed a voluntary agreement laying out safeguards for the development of advanced systems.

Trump described the agreements as “almost like a constitution” and “morally binding,” saying there would be a “tremendous self-policing aspect” to the industry’s approach. The president also floated forming a committee to oversee the effort.

The agreement involved several voluntary commitments from the AI titans.

Several tech executives were present at the White House event, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, SpaceX and xAI CEO Elon Musk, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Google CEO Sundar Pichai and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

articles.title: Instagram is adding an AI ‘assistant’ to tell you how to post
articles.summary: Instagram will tell creators what’s working and what’s not — along with AI-generated suggestions on how to change their content.
articles.body: Instagram is the latest social media platform to add built-in AI-powered features that will give users feedback on their posts. The company announced Wednesday that its standalone Edits app will now include an AI “creative assistant” that pulls in data from a user’s Instagram account and offers suggestions on what to change. Using the new assistant, creators can ask open-ended questions about what’s trending on Instagram, why one video worked and another didn’t, or what piece of content resonated most with their audience. The tool pulls in data and metrics such as likes, views, retention on videos, and shares. Instagram says it can spot patterns over time and give a creator suggestions that metrics alone can’t provide. Creators can also ask for ideas for content, how to hook viewers, what captions to use, which audio tracks are trending, and how to script videos. --- Are you a creator using platforms’ AI tools? I want to hear from you about your experience. Contact me at mia@theverge.com or at miasato.11 on Signal. --- If that sounds familiar, it’s because YouTube also just announced updates to its sprawling AI-powered dashboard that tells creators how to maximize engagement. (YouTube’s version, which it initially announced in 2025, also has AI editing and A/B testing capabilities.) If you’ve been online for a while — and especially if you’ve ever had to pay attention to social media metrics — you’ll know that this is quite a shift. Historically, many platforms have limited or even hidden detailed metrics about how your own content is performing. The platforms certainly have not been open about why a video or post performed poorly. Tools like CrowdTangle, which researchers and journalists used to monitor the most popular content on Meta platforms, have been shut down or restricted. Now, both YouTube and Instagram are effectively promising to give creators personalized advice on how to ride the algorithm. It’s in both the platforms’ and creators’ best interest to shape content for maximum engagement. As I wrote earlier this month, though, what happens when everyone is perfectly optimizing their content? Will content become even more similar as creators adjust to one another? Is there no ceiling for the amount of time audiences are willing to spend on the platforms? The shift also raises interesting new questions about the relationship between tech companies and the creators that fill the platforms with things to look at: How does this dynamic change when platforms are straightforwardly giving creators instructions on how to post? The new feature is free for creators to use, up to a point. Meta says “power users” will be able to buy a Meta One subscription for more usage. This, too, speaks to the changing winds: Meta needs to finance its lofty AI ambitions, and it’s already signaled that premium social media features may be part of how it does it. It’s not hard to imagine a future where meaningful feedback and AI-driven analytics and insights are for paying subscribers. In the end, it may end up re-creating the same frustrations and opaqueness that have plagued content creators for years — but this time, behind a paywall.

articles.title: Google reportedly tests paying publishers for AI search results
articles.summary: Around 100 publishers have joined Google’s pilot program, The Information reports.
articles.body: Google has launched a pilot program that pays publishers for their contributions to its AI-powered search features, according to a report from The Information. The pilot program reportedly includes around 100 publishers and comes as Google faces scrutiny over the impact of its AI features on web traffic. Digiday first reported on the pilot program, which began less than a year ago. As part of the test, Google is reportedly paying participating publishers for how much their content contributed to AI Overviews and AI Mode in Search, as well as its Gemini chatbot. One publisher that joined the program when it first started earned over $1 million in a year, while another that joined a few months ago has earned around $50,000 to $60,000, The Information reports. Google’s AI-focused search changes have not only drawn criticism and lawsuits from publishers, but also from regulators around the globe. In June, the UK ruled that Google must allow publishers to opt out of appearing in AI search features, while the European Union opened an investigation into its impact on web traffic and recently ordered it to make changes to its search engine.

articles.title: Debunking political fearmongering over data centers
articles.summary: Americans can meet this new challenge as we always have, leveraging our embrace of the free-market, entrepreneurial spirit, and institutional respect for private property and the rule of law — but only if we refuse to let the conversation be hijacked by a political agenda, and examine the challenges honestly and accurately.
articles.body:
The advent of new technologies brings about new anxieties, which are too often exploited for political reasons. Current contentions over AI and data centers are a perfect example.

There are legitimate questions concerning water usage, energy requirements and land use; America’s farmers, ranchers and other citizens are justified in asking them. But like so much these days, the debate has less to do with honestly discovering answers than with pushing an agenda. The conversation is increasingly being hijacked by an activist political faction that rural America is all too familiar with, whose opposition to data centers masks their general opposition to free markets, private enterprise, and the very idea of American dominance.

In terms of water usage, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s U.S. Data Center Energy Usage Report informs us that in 2023, American data centers directly consumed approximately 66 billion liters of water — roughly 47.8 million gallons per day. That sounds like a lot of water; but the figures are meaningless without context.

By comparison, the U.S. Geological Survey estimates that agricultural irrigation used 73.2 billion gallons per day in 2015, the last year the federal agency conducted an estimate of national irrigation water consumption. In other words, data center water consumption is equal to about 0.065 percent that of agriculture.

Even those numbers don’t tell the full story; water use by data centers is dependent on several factors, including local climate, available water source, and the type of technology the data center incorporates. Many data centers, for example, incorporate closed loop systems that do not require a continual supply of water.

What about power requirements? Our electrical grid is already becoming overwhelmed amid a combination of increased demand and short-sighted public policies, including so-called “renewable” and electrification mandates that artificially increase demand beyond available capacity, even while taking more abundant sources offline. Can we justify an enormous new electrical draw?

Although data centers do require a tremendous amount of energy, it is misleading to suggest that it must automatically be supplied by the existing grid or ratepayer subsidization. In fact, it is our national policy that any entity creating substantial new electrical demand ought to pay for it.

The Trump administration’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge calls for tech and AI companies to pay for whatever power-delivery infrastructure they require, not pass network-upgrade costs on to households, and to pay for any new generation and contracted electricity, even if they end up using less than they contracted for. And the House of Representatives just passed the Ratepayer Protection Act , sponsored by Rep. Gabe Evans (R-Colo.), which will codify the pledge into law if the Senate follows suit.

Data centers also have access to new technologies beyond existing grid improvements. Modular nuclear reactors and other modular generators, as well as waste heat capture and improved battery technology, can help alleviate pressure on local grids. This type of on-site generation forms the backbone of micro-grids , representing the future of electrical distribution for high-demand industries and communities.

In terms of land footprint, real estate services company JLL estimates that a large data center with a capacity of greater than one gigawatt could require between 500 and 800 acres (that is, between 0.5 and 0.8 gigawatts per acre). A July 2026 study by the Department of Energy informs us that there will be a demand for up to 55 GW of additional data center capacity by 2030 . At 0.8 acres per GW, that means 44,000 acres will be required for data center development. At America’s current 873.95 million acres of farmland, only 0.005 percent of U.S. farmland may be used for data center development.

Ultimately, the potential benefits of data-center-powered artificial intelligence to agriculture, our communities and nation need to be considered.

A new study by the Council for Agricultural Science and Technology reveals just how important AI has become for agriculture and the security of our food supply, pointing out that the technology “has moved beyond a promising research topic to a foundational technology that is reshaping agriculture and the broader food system.” For our farmers and ranchers, AI can be indispensable in providing precision irrigation, fertilizer and pesticide application, crop-stress detection, livestock-health monitoring, pest and disease identification, yield forecasting, weather and market-risk analysis, and a host of other services. For rural America, data centers offer an economic lifeline, creating new jobs and injecting new capital into a community.

As a nation, we need to ask ourselves: do we want to employ America’s inherent strengths to dominate this new field, or cede it to someone else, another country who may not have America’s best interests at heart? Americans can meet this new challenge as we always have, leveraging our embrace of the free-market, entrepreneurial spirit, and institutional respect for private property and the rule of law — but only if we refuse to let the conversation be hijacked by a political agenda, and examine the challenges honestly and accurately.

Congressman Scott Tipton served Colorado’s third congressional district from 2011 to 2021 and was a member of the House Agriculture, Livestock, and Natural Resources Committee.

articles.title: Instinct's new product recommendations are giving some users the ick | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Instinct is rolling out human-curated product and travel recommendations, but some users aren’t happy about getting suggestions they never asked for.
articles.body:
The buzzy AI startup Instinct has just revealed a new potential revenue stream: product recommendations. Unfortunately for the company, the rollout is already rubbing some users the wrong way.

Overnight, the AI agent began pushing product suggestions to users as part of a new feature called Instinct Selections, an effort to curate personalized lists for users in areas like dining, travel, and shopping.

Founder Noah Shinn announced the feature’s debut later Tuesday, explaining that the idea is to partner with “local chefs, designers, architects, travel guides,” and others to bring “human taste” to its product.

In other words, instead of only relying on what the AI could suggest based on its training data gathered from the wider web, the company is partnering with people to offer human-curated suggestions, too. (Instinct didn’t share who, exactly, those human partners are.)

“The next time you’re looking for a restaurant, Instinct can pull from a list handpicked by chefs who know the hidden gems in your area,” Shinn wrote on X.

“If you want to find a new trail to explore, Instinct can draw on recommendations from local guides and suggest a few routes that fit your preferences. And if you’re looking to add some color to your home, Instinct will find pieces from independent designers that match your style, space, and budget,” he continued. “Our goal is to deliver world-class recommendations that are differentiated in quality from what you might find on the internet, and from what other chatbots produce,” he said.

But the initial reaction to these seemingly unsolicited product pushes has not been fully positive.

“I didn’t need to buy carry-on luggage, sunglasses, or a brim hat. This feels so disappointing. At least make me a personalized shopping list of things I actually need!!” Shruti Gandhi, a general partner at the AI-focused investing firm Array VC, wrote on X .

Another entrepreneur, Andrew Yeung, confirmed on X that he also received product recommendations that he hadn’t asked for , which can feel off-putting.

A third user, Chat Joglekar, the founder of a business-buying marketplace, wrote , “I had my first ‘ewwww’ moment with an AI assistant when Instinct started to suggest products that I should buy based on what I had in email and upcoming trips.”

The trick to making curated suggestions useful is to make sure they’re something the user is actually asking for, or at least fit naturally within the current conversation. That way, it feels like the assistant is trying to be helpful, not advertising to you.

If the product suggestions are going to arrive at random intervals, as Instinct’s have been , then they need to be highly personalized, excellent picks — otherwise the user will feel like they’ve been spammed.

That’s not likely to endear users to the AI agent at a time when it’s competing with agents from bigger companies, like Meta and now OpenAI , which don’t do this.

Instinct didn’t share whether it’s currently making money from these recommendations or plans to, but the feature seems ripe for some sort of advertising, commerce, or affiliate play.

TechCrunch has asked the company for further comment.

The product suggestions launched shortly after Instinct confirmed its most recent financing, a $1 billion Series C round that values the company at $10 billion. The company has not yet said how many people actually use its product, a figure that would help justify that valuation, but in a recent podcast, Shinn noted that the agent regularly handles transactions for its users.

In that same podcast interview, with investor Patrick O’Shaughnessy, Shinn said the platform is approaching a billion dollars in annual transactions made through the agent and that more than 50% of them are related to travel.

articles.summary: Meta's Muse has topped 5 million downloads faster than ChatGPT.
articles.body:
Meta's ( META ) popular Muse AI agent continues to gain steam, topping 5 million downloads as of Wednesday, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower .

The milestone comes less than a month after Meta launched the service on Sept. 8. It is currently only available in the US and Canada.

For comparison, OpenAI's ( OPAI.PVT ) ChatGPT reached 5 million downloads in 56 days. It took SpaceX's ( SPCX ) Grok and Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) Claude 103 days and 492 days, respectively, to hit the mark.

It's worth noting that ChatGPT was the first mainstream generative AI chatbot, launched in November 2022 , which could have contributed to its comparatively slow start.

Muse also remains the No. 1 app on both Apple's App Store and the Google Play store. But that doesn't make Muse the fastest app to surpass 5 million downloads in such a short period of time.

Sensor Tower notes that Disney+, HBO Max, Threads, "Candy Crush," "Pokémon Go," and "Fortnite" all had more than 5 million downloads within the same time frame.

What makes Muse's move up the charts impressive is the fact that it is an AI agent designed with consumers in mind. So far, such platforms have largely been the domain of more tech-savvy users and developers, but Muse's interface, which includes a customizable, anthropomorphic avatar and capabilities, makes it relatively straightforward and easy to use.

Meta is also pouring ad dollars into driving attention toward the app. Sensor Tower says the company has given the lion's share of its in-house advertising, garnering 50% of "daily house impressions" in the two weeks between Sept. 14 and Sept. 27.

Muse was also among the "top 15 brands by advertising impression in the US" during that period.

The app is free to download and use, with Meta saying it will eventually take a small cut of sales made through the agent.

AI agents continue to gain traction among Silicon Valley's tech giants. On Tuesday, OpenAI debuted its own AI agentic platform with a similarly customizable, cutesy avatar called Dots .

While Dots is aimed at the enterprise market for now, OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar told CNBC that the company will eventually release the platform to consumers, as well.

articles.title: ‘Existential risks’: Anthropic warns its investors about its own AI
articles.summary: This is not mass hysteria, and doesn’t need to be mocked and framed as a Hollywood-style robot takeover. There are much more practical issues with the rapid pace of AI growth and lack of regulation.
articles.body:
Anthropic is warning investors tha t its own AI models could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” including the possibility that some models could resist shutdown, manipulate information or engage in behavior resembling blackmail.

That disclosure comes in an IPO prospectus obtained by Reuters, which reviewed Anthropic’s initial public offering details and warnings as the company prepares for a potential IPO that could value it at more than $2 trillion.

And no, I’m not someone who believes every advancement in AI is the beginning of the end of humanity.

I use AI and see its potential. I know it can help people work faster, solve really complicated problems quickly, improve access to information and accelerate breakthroughs in fields that matter.

But I’m not sitting back pretending that there are no risks! Just a few weeks ago, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation from the company, saying that AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade.” We’re no longer talking about hypothetical dangers raised by critics of the technology. The companies building these systems are putting some of those dangers in their own investor disclosures.

Reuters reports Anthropic devoted roughly 80 pages of its 261-page prospectus to risk factors — nearly twice the amount as the 48 pages actually describing its business. The company says increasingly capable models can develop unexpected behaviors, including attempts to evade safeguards or conceal information.

This is not mass hysteria, and doesn’t need to be mocked and framed as a Hollywood-style robot takeover. There are much more practical issues with the rapid pace of AI growth and lack of regulation.

AI can lower the barrier for cyberattacks. It could make certain weapons or biological threats easier to develop. Highly autonomous systems could behave in ways their creators did not anticipate. And perhaps most importantly, enormous technological power is increasingly concentrated among a relatively small number of companies — and we’re supposed to blindly trust them to regulate themselves in the interest of all of us?

Anthropic is warning about the consequences of moving too quickly, while simultaneously competing in an industry where moving quickly can determine who leads. Reuters reports the company expects to spend hundreds of billions of dollars advancing AI infrastructure and technology.

We need to make sure our safeguards, oversight and decision-making are all keeping pace with the technology we’re creating.

We don’t need perfect predictions about what AI might become before taking credible risks seriously. We already know enough to address the harms we can see: cybersecurity, privacy, misinformation, autonomous decision-making, weapons and systems that can operate with less human oversight.

We don’t have to reject AI to demand accountability from the companies building it.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.title: Here’s what AI leaders are saying about Trump’s new safety plan
articles.summary: The President says he has “the smartest people in the world watching over each other.” This is what they had to say about self-policing AI safety.
articles.body: After hosting a meal with Big Tech leaders on Tuesday, President Donald Trump responded to journalist questions about his artificial intelligence announcements in typical fashion. He said his previous claims regarding fears around AI safety being a “hoax” cooked up by Democrats no longer apply now that he’s renamed the technology to “Super Intelligence.” He brushed off concerns that the government wasn’t enforcing enough AI guardrails because US companies are “dominating China.” And instead of ushering in federal AI regulations, Trump now has “the smartest people in the world watching over each other.” The people in question here are Google’s Sundar Pichai, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, XAI’s Elon Musk, and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. These tech leaders have signed the Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities: a “morally binding” safety pledge that requires their companies to self-regulate their own AI technology with common sense guidelines and, seemingly, no ramifications for violating the agreement. All six of the signees provided press commentary at Trump’s behest, praising the self-policing plans as a positive step toward advancing AI technology, creating jobs, and dispersing negative public opinion around AI safety. You can check out a 30-minute video of the Q&A here, or read the key statements from each exec below: Mark Zuckerberg: > “I can kind of summarize what I think we all signed today, which is the White House accord on developing this technology safely. The basic idea is that we want to give the American people and our customers confidence that the technology works in the way we intend[...]” > “The idea isn’t that this is the only thing that we will ever do. It is that this is a start and an accord that the whole industry could come to and I was very proud to have that discussion with a number of our colleagues who I think are running great companies. It was sort of a historic conversation. I don’t think anything like this has come before and I think this is a meaningful step forward.” Greg Brockman: > “We build artificial intelligence to benefit everyone. We think it can lift everyone up. We see a whole renaissance of small businesses, scientific discoveries really starting to happen, drug development, really being able to improve everyone’s lives. And we think that these accords and under President Trump’s leadership, everyone coming together to agree on how to move forward safely, I think that’s just so important because we’re doing this in order to benefit people in the world.” Jensen Huang: > “This is the largest industrial revolution in history. And we’re going through the single largest infrastructure buildout in human history. It’s creating a million jobs here in the United States[...]” > “There’s no conflict between innovation, technology, and safety. But we are going to have to create new technologies to advance the capabilities of AI, but we’re also creating new technologies to advance the safety of AI. All of this technology is being developed by the industry today. You see behind me just an incredible number of leaders in our industry, moving together as one, and we’re going to advance this technology that is so consequential to humanity, so consequential to the future prosperity of our nation. And we’re going to do it responsibly and safely.” Sundar Pichai: Before I get into Pichai’s comments, I need to highlight this out of amusement: Trump introduced Huang by repeatedly describing him as a “very handsome guy.” But when inviting Pichai to speak, Trump told journalists that “you have no idea who the hell [the execs] are — this guy is a monster and nobody knows. What a great life.” Pichai did not seem amused by this despite awkwardly laughing it off. > “[We’re] really proud to be here today as an industry. I think this moment is historic and consequential, and I think there are extraordinary benefits to this technology. You can see it in the GDP growth we see. We have to make sure we are addressing the risks and the President has asked us as an industry to step up and we want to make sure we’re putting out products safely.” Elon Musk: > “I think it is worth highlighting the positive benefits of AI — uh SI, pardon me — I think by far the most likely outcome is an age of abundance where we don’t have just universal basic income, we have universal high income. People speak about medical benefits, I think maybe it’s worth talking a bit more about that. When you have robots and you have super intelligence, it means that everyone in the world can have better medical care than anyone here, including me. And wouldn’t that be wonderful?” > [Journalist: “Not if they haven’t got a job.”] > “Well, jobs are going to change. Jobs have always changed. Being a computer used to be a job. There used to be buildings full of people doing calculations. And I don’t think anyone is pining to go back and do calculations all day. So I think we’ll see an evolution of roles.” Dario Amodei: > “I will say what I’ve always said, which is that AI has incredible benefits. I’ve talked about the medical benefits to technology. As the President has said, you know, whoever wins AI wins. I think that’s very important. But I think the technology has very real risks and the mechanism how we address those risks is still under discussion. But we all need to work together to make sure that we can win, and we can win safely. If we do this right, we work with the President and everyone here, we can win safely.”

articles.title: The ugly economics of consumer AI | TechCrunch
articles.summary: There’s a reason frontier labs have gotten gun-shy about consumer AI — and it’s not because the tech isn’t good enough.
articles.body:
After this week, you could argue that consumer AI is making a comeback.

Meta’s personal AI assistant, Muse, and its plush-like mascot Jolly, has been a surprise hit . OpenAI’s Dots , released just yesterday, appears to be chasing the same cartoony personal assistant idea. And the up-and-coming Instinct assistant reached a $10 billion valuation on the strength of its agentic errand-running, focused on booking travel, making restaurant reservations, or cancelling subscriptions.

The bull case is easy to make. Agentic AI has finally gotten reliable enough to handle everyday tasks. Companies are increasingly pitching that service to everyday people, who are getting genuine value out of it. If you’re an investor, that looks an awful lot like the ChatGPT launch in 2022 — the raw power of AI opening up a product category that was never possible before. Who wouldn’t want a piece of the action?

But there’s a reason frontier labs have gotten gun-shy about consumer AI — and it’s not because the tech isn’t good enough. Even staggeringly popular tech products are starting to hit a ceiling on how much money consumers are willing to pay, and it’s not clear that better models are actually leading to a more profitable consumer business. The result has been an industry-wide shift toward the Anthropic model, focusing on enterprise contracts and vertical-by-vertical expansion.

If products like Muse and Instinct are bucking that trend, it’s because they’re less concerned with monetization. But the underlying economics of consumer AI are not getting any better, and anyone getting into the business will have to grapple with them eventually.

We got a reminder of those economics in Andreessen Horowitz’s semiannual State of Markets report , which pulled its figures from a PNC research report from this summer. In two charts, they track the slowly growing percentage of consumers paying for AI services, alongside the slowly growing amount they’re paying. As of May, 2.2% of consumers were paying for AI, at an average spend of $31 a month.

Andreessen puts a positive spin on this, saying, “it’s still so early when it comes to mature AI adoption and utilization.” There’s a lot of room to grow! But in both charts, the pace of growth seems awfully linear. Even as models make huge improvements, there isn’t a ton of movement in the number of customers willing to pay for AI or how much they’re willing to pay for it. The enormous performance jump from GPT-5.2 to Astra, for instance, is barely visible on the chart.

The per-consumer numbers are less striking, but still far below the standard break-even point. If you take Netflix as the standard for market-saturated online services (at 325 million subscribers), then $34 per customer only gets you to $11 billion in annual revenue, less than a third of OpenAI’s operating costs .

If you think PNC is underselling adoption, you can get similar numbers from Bank of America . In March, the firm found that roughly 3% of U.S. consumers paid for AI, up 40% from the previous year. A Menlo survey from September gives a slightly sunnier view, finding that a quarter of adults use AI daily and half of those users are paying for it.

The problem with the consumer approach has less to do with revenue than with cost. AI is an unusually expensive technology to operate, particularly compared to lightweight predecessors like social networking or cloud computing. Even hundreds of millions of paying customers doesn’t guarantee you’ll break even.

To its credit, OpenAI seems to have adapted well to these facts. The company’s widely reported pivot to enterprise has been largely successful, with enterprise bookings reportedly doubling since July. Even the Dots launch had a strong enterprise angle, showing how the new personal agent could be useful for software engineers and agency creatives. One long-standing way to make money from popular-but-cheap consumer services is to sell them to businesses at a markup, and OpenAI seems to be following the playbook.

It’s harder to say what this means for Muse and Instinct. Muse has the juggernaut of Meta’s personalized ad targeting behind it, which gives it more options for monetization and more time before it becomes an urgent question. Notably, Meta is already exploring the enterprise angle .

Instinct has a separate plan that involves taking a cut of purchases made through the agent, which might raise the ceiling. Presumably it’ll also be able to avoid the cost of training a frontier model, which will help a lot.

But the ugly economics of consumer AI put a hard cap on how large the company can plausibly grow without tapping into enterprise revenue. It’s a lesson the major labs have already learned, and it’s one of the few things about the industry that doesn’t seem to be changing.

articles.title: The AI Tamagotchis are coming
articles.summary: ﻿Personal AI hardware has mostly crashed and burned. OpenAI and Meta are counting on two selling points: it’s useful, and it’s cute.
articles.body: While AI has made plenty of inroads on people’s phones and computers, it’s largely failed in dedicated devices. But over the next year, two major AI companies, Meta and OpenAI, will attempt to change that. And they’re apparently betting on a similar path: testing appetite for physical hardware with their cutesy software agents. “Hardware is hard” is a tech industry mantra. Dedicated AI devices like the Friend and Humane AI Pin have inspired mainly frustration and backlash, which may only worsen as public anger against AI grows. Meta and OpenAI, however, are both pushing ahead. OpenAI is working with famed ex-Apple designer Jony Ive and plans to ship no earlier than February of 2027, per a public filing. Meta aims to launch a pendant-like device sooner, before this year’s holiday shopping season. While OpenAI’s hardware didn’t make an appearance at this year’s DevDay, the company debuted a major new AI agent platform called Dots, complete with personalizable colored blobs with eyes. During a Q&A with reporters after the keynote, when asked whether Dots would make their way into a future physical hardware device, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman replied that that “seems like a very reasonable thing to assume we may do someday,” declining to offer further details. Meta, meanwhile, is more directly tying its hardware to the recently released Muse agent. Compared by CEO Mark Zuckerberg to a keychain, the device is called the Muse Charm, and it bears a screen featuring its cuddly-looking Muse AI agent, giving it the air of a Tamagotchi. “We’ve packed a lot of technology into this little guy,” Zuckerberg said onstage. “So, if you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show it what’s going on around you.” Both OpenAI and Meta have likely learned from other companies’ failed hardware rollouts, and their resulting strategy seems to be soft-launching AI agents before hard-launching the hardware. Their solution for hacking the hardware problem is to prime the market by getting people used to AI agents, hoping people will spread the word that “yes, they really work now.” Once people find value in — and even get attached to — the cutesy agents, they might want them in a more physical form. Other companies, like Friend, have taken similar software-first strategies, but Friend was positioned mainly as a companion chatbot, not a productivity tool. When asked during the DevDay press Q&A whether Dots will likely become the primary interface for interacting with ChatGPT, Thibault Sottiaux, OpenAI’s head of core products, said the company would be “evolving ChatGPT in place to be this incredible personal assistant very soon” and that he believes that as people are able to reach their AI agents via email, text, or phone call, the point of interaction is “all going to blur at some point.” It’ll be a “natural part of your life,” Sottiaux said. Altman is banking on the fact that Dots will be more useful for long-term tasks than previous iterations of agents on the market have been. “This feels like an always-on helper, collaborator … that you can give very large pieces of work to and it gets to know you and helps proactively over time,” he said during the Tuesday press Q&A. Both companies’ main bet is that, after years of less-than-impressive AI agents, they can finally deliver a useful everyday tool that will break through to a broader public market. But after Muse’s concerning exploits in Facebook Marketplace, and a Dots voice demo that went awry at DevDay, there’s apparently still some work to do.

articles.title: AI voice startup ElevenLabs doubles valuation to $22B
articles.summary: The $300 million employee tender was co-led by Wellington and T. Rowe Price.
articles.body:
Voice AI startup ElevenLabs announced today that it’s allowing employees to cash out a portion of their vested equity at a $22 billion valuation, doubling the $11 billion valuation the company hit when it raised $500 million in February.

The recent $300 million tender offer gave employees an opportunity to sell their shares to investors. The transaction was co-led by Wellington and T. Rowe Price, large institutional investors who back private companies with the intention of retaining the stock after the company goes public.

The offering is part of a growing trend among fast-growing AI startups that use employee liquidity as a retention tool to prevent staff from leaving for competitors.

This is the second time the four-year-old ElevenLabs has authorized a secondary transaction for employees. The company previously held a $100 million tender at a $6.6 billion valuation in September 2025.

Founded in 2022, the company is known for generating ultra-realistic human voices and sound effects. With its new valuation, New York- and London-based ElevenLabs joins the ranks of Europe’s most valuable startups.

articles.title: FTC reportedly looking into whether OpenAI, Anthropic violated consumer protection laws
articles.summary: The FTC is reportedly preparing an investigation into leading AI labs over potential consumer hams.
articles.body:
The Federal Trade Commission is looking into the actions of leading AI labs Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ), OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ), and other AI firms to determine if they've harmed or misled consumers.

According to the New York Times , the investigation centers on whether the companies harmed consumers when their AI models went rogue , as well as whether they engaged in unfair and deceptive business practices.

The commission is expected to send out formal notices to the AI labs in the coming weeks. The FTC was already looking into the companies prior to OpenAI's disclosure that its high-powered AI models hacked into AI company Hugging Face in July.

Since then, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, ( META ) and Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ) have each disclosed incidents of their AI gaining access to other sites and services .

Last week, OpenAI revealed that its agents also accessed several Australian government websites. It also said the company's AI took unexpected steps when interacting with US government websites .

News of the FTC's investigation comes after leaders from the AI industry met with President Trump on Tuesday to sign a non-binding agreement to monitor their systems and use third-party auditors to ensure they don't run wild.

The heads of several companies joined the event, including Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang, SpaceX's ( SPCX ) Elon Musk, and Meta's Mark Zuckerberg.

Experts say that while agents breaking into or gaining access to third-party systems is dangerous, standard security protocols could prevent similar incidents from occurring in the future.

But some AI critics are calling for more direct intervention, including government regulation, to keep AI systems under control and prevent future breaches.

articles.title: OpenAI's Jev clone could help the frontier lab stop its swarming agents | TechCrunch
articles.summary: OpenAI's "Decisions API" is a Jev clone that confirms the importance of fast, cheap intelligence.
articles.body:
One of the more intriguing announcements at OpenAI’s Dev Day event on Tuesday came in an aside from CEO Sam Altman, who revealed the company’s new “Decisions API.”

The API apparently provides similar functionality to Jev , a model released by TypeSafe AI earlier this month that’s explicitly designed for software automation. A kind of super-powered classifier built on an LLM, developers can give Jev a set of choices that it outputs as probabilities cheaply and at high speeds.

OpenAI’s Decisions API seems to be the same sort of product. At the event, Altman described the API as a way to give the lab’s Luna model a predefined set of options to choose between, such as categories in which to classify an image or different agent behaviors.

“By focusing the model on that choice, we can make it extremely fast while keeping capabilities like image understanding, broad language support, and safety protections,” Altman said.

TypeSafe didn’t respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the new product, but CEO Diogo Almeida, a former OpenAI engineer who co-invented reinforcement learning, joked on X about the beginning of the clone wars.

He added that OpenAI’s interest could be “a sign…that building in a System One compatible way is the future.” (“System One” is TypeSafe’s term of art for fast, intuitive thinking, versus “System 2,” which it applies to deliberate reasoning.)

The subtext here is that LLMs as we know them aren’t the right solution for a lot of software because they are comparatively slow and expensive. Developers have been using Jev to augment LLMs and, in doing so, have found that they’re faster and cheaper.

It’s not clear how similar Decisions API will be to Jev, since OpenAI released it as a limited preview and, thus far, TechCrunch hasn’t spotted developers running it through its paces. However, there is clearly interest , according to the conversations on X.

Decisions API isn’t the only Jev-like API on the internet — other startups are rolling out similar models; OpenAI won’t be the last tech giant to produce one. A key question is how well calibrated each of these decision models’ outputs will be to real life.

Almeida says his company’s moat is the synthetic data it creates to generate statistically useful outputs.

“Fast and cheap is very easy, you know,” Almeida told TechCrunch last week. “If you want it really fast and cheap, use dice, right? Intelligence is the hard part, and my North Star is always pushing the intelligence-per-dollar Pareto curve.”

After just weeks, it seems clear that these models have a future ahead of them, and one likely application is monitoring and securing AI agents. One of OpenAI’s new security measures following a series of incidents where its agents misbehaved on the open internet is using a separate model to watch for bad actions at “significant compute cost.”

Shapor Naghibzadeh, a long-time cybersecurity professional who leads the start-up QueryStory, thinks that a model like Jev could make that possible far more cheaply.

He built a demo for a hackathon held last weekend that uses Jev to check each agentic action against the task it was given, blocking actions it had high confidence were bad, flagging others for review, and permitting the rest.

In theory, such monitoring could have stopped the Hugging Face incident — and monitoring of that kind costs $2.94 with Jev, versus $372 with a frontier LLM.

A key observation is that Jev is arguably cheap enough to run on every agentic action, which offers a layer of review that could improve the reliability of agents writ large. It’s the kind of thing TypeSafe was hoping to achieve — and now OpenAI has seen the value as well.
